planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring into well-drained to seasonally moist soil in full sun; spreads by fine rhizomes to form a low, dense sod-like groundcover.

directions: Mat muhly is a low, rhizomatous native grass that spreads into a dense, knotted sod of fine blue-green blades rarely exceeding a foot tall. Narrow, tightly appressed gray-green flower spikes appear in early summer and are inconspicuous compared to the showy plumes of pink muhly relatives. Found naturally from Alaska and Canada south through the western US to Baja California, it tolerates both seasonally moist meadows and drier upland sites once established. Its low, spreading habit makes it useful as a native lawn substitute, erosion-control groundcover, or filler between stepping stones in low-traffic areas.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun to light shade; native to the uplands of northern Mexico and hardy to roughly 15-20F once established.

directions: Soft blue muhly forms a graceful, weeping mound of fine, velvety, steel-blue foliage that blushes reddish-purple after the first cold snap. In late summer and early fall, pale lilac flower plumes rise well above the foliage on slender stems before drying to a warm buff color that persists into winter. Native to the dry uplands of northern Mexico, it is extremely drought tolerant once established and thrives in lean, well-drained soil. Its soft color and cascading texture make it a striking accent or mass planting in xeriscape and Southwestern-style gardens.

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring in dry, rocky or loamy, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; native to pinyon-juniper and ponderosa pine grasslands of the southern Rocky Mountains and slow to establish but long-lived once rooted in.

directions: Spike muhly is a compact, warm-season bunchgrass forming tight clumps 1-2 feet across, with narrow, upright flower spikes that appear yellowish-green in early summer and mature to tan. Unlike the plumed pink and purple muhly grasses grown for fall color, spike muhly is valued for its fine, wiry texture, tidy clumping habit, and toughness in cold, high-elevation gardens. Native to rocky slopes and open woodlands of the southern Rocky Mountains from Colorado and Utah south to Arizona and New Mexico, it tolerates poor, rocky, alkaline soils and is very drought tolerant once established. It is well suited to native plant gardens, rock gardens, and high-elevation xeriscapes where more tender muhly species struggle with winter cold.
sources: City of Fort Collins Recommended Plant List

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; native to sandy prairies and plains from Texas and Oklahoma north to Kansas and Colorado.

directions: Sand muhly is a fine-textured, clump-forming native bunchgrass reaching up to about 28 inches tall, with slender blue-green blades and airy, understated flower panicles that appear from late spring through fall and carry subtle purple tinges in the lemmas. It is native to sandy prairies, plains, and open grasslands across Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, Colorado, Arizona, and New Mexico, where it thrives in loose, well-drained, sandy soils. Highly drought tolerant once established, it works well in naturalistic prairie plantings, sandy-soil rock gardens, and native grass meadows. Its long bloom season and fine texture provide a soft, airy foil for coarser-textured perennials.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring in well-drained, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; native to open desert grasslands and rocky slopes of Arizona and New Mexico.

directions: Arizona muhly is a compact, fine-textured native bunchgrass growing to about 20 inches tall, producing airy flower panicles in shades of green, purple, and brown from late summer into fall. It is native to open desert grasslands, rocky slopes, and sandy drainages across Arizona and New Mexico, where it is well adapted to lean, gravelly soils and minimal supplemental water. Its small stature and muted plume color make it a good choice for rock gardens, desert-adapted borders, and native plant collections where a subtler counterpart to showier pink muhly grasses is desired.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with room to reach its full 3-foot spread; tolerates colder winters than the straight species.

directions: Undaunted Sure Thing is a notably cold-hardy selection of deer grass, discovered by plantswoman Lauren Springer in the Canadian River canyon of northeastern New Mexico and introduced by High Country Gardens. It forms a dense, rounded mound of fine sage-green foliage topped from midsummer through fall by tall, silvery-tan flower spikes that create a fountain-like, shooting effect above the clump. Hardy to USDA zone 4, it extends the reliable garden range of deer grass well beyond that of the straight species while retaining excellent drought tolerance and deer resistance once established. It works well as a structural accent or in mass plantings in xeriscapes, native plant gardens, and high-elevation landscapes.

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring in sandy to rocky, well-drained soil in full sun; spreads by rhizomes into a low mat and is native to open sandy meadows, canyon bottoms, and gypsum flats of the southwestern US.

directions: Creeping muhly is a low, mat-forming native grass that spreads by rhizomes into a dense groundcover rarely more than 16 inches tall. Narrow flower spikes in muted green and brown tones appear from late summer through fall, valued more for texture than showy color. Native to open sandy meadows, canyon bottoms, calcareous rocky flats, and gypsum flats across Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, Texas, and Utah, it is highly drought tolerant once established and tolerates poor, mineral soils. Its low, spreading habit suits it to erosion control on slopes, native lawn alternatives, and filling gaps between stepping stones or boulders in dry gardens.
